solution:
The radius of a nucleus of mass number \(A\) is \(R = R_0 A^{1/3}\), where \(R_0\) is the same constant for every nucleus. Taking the ratio for gold \((A = 197)\) and silver \((A = 107)\), \(R_0\) cancels:

\(\dfrac{R_{\text{Au}}}{R_{\text{Ag}}} = \left(\dfrac{A_{\text{Au}}}{A_{\text{Ag}}}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\dfrac{197}{107}\right)^{1/3}\)

Now \(\dfrac{197}{107} = 1.841\), and \((1.841)^{1/3} = 1.226\).

\(\dfrac{R_{\text{Au}}}{R_{\text{Ag}}} \approx 1.23\) (a pure number, no unit) — the gold nucleus has a radius about \(1.23\) times that of the silver nucleus.

Consider a nucleus of mass number \(A\). It contains \(A\) nucleons of nearly equal mass, so its mass is

\(M \approx A\,m_N\), where \(m_N \approx 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\,\text{kg}\) is the average mass of one nucleon \((\approx 1\,\text{u})\); the mass defect due to binding is only a fraction of a per cent and is neglected.

Treating the nucleus as a sphere of radius \(R = R_0 A^{1/3}\), its volume is

\(V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A\)

Hence the nuclear matter density is

\(\rho = \dfrac{M}{V} = \dfrac{A\,m_N}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \dfrac{3\,m_N}{4\pi R_0^3}\)

The factor \(A\) cancels because the mass rises in direct proportion to \(A\) while the volume, being proportional to \(R^3 = R_0^3 A\), rises in the same proportion. What is left contains only the constants \(m_N\) and \(R_0\), so \(\rho\) is the same for every nucleus, light or heavy. Physically this reflects the saturation of the short-range nuclear force: a nucleon binds only to its immediate neighbours, so nucleons sit at a fixed average spacing instead of being drawn closer together as \(A\) grows.

Substituting \(R_0 = 1.2\,\text{fm} = 1.2 \times 10^{-15}\,\text{m}\):

\(\rho = \dfrac{3 \times (1.66 \times 10^{-27}\,\text{kg})}{4\pi (1.2 \times 10^{-15}\,\text{m})^3} = \dfrac{1.66 \times 10^{-27}\,\text{kg}}{7.24 \times 10^{-45}\,\text{m}^3} = 2.29 \times 10^{17}\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\)

Nuclear matter density \(\rho = \dfrac{3\,m_N}{4\pi R_0^3} \approx 2.3 \times 10^{17}\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\), independent of \(A\).
